An aspirant is a person who strongly wants to achieve something big — a high goal, an important position, a title, or a prestigious status — and is actively working toward it.

The two things that define an aspirant are:

  • They have a serious ambition — a burning desire for something meaningful or elevated.
  • They have not yet achieved it — they are still on the journey, still striving.

Think of it this way: an aspirant is someone standing at the bottom of the mountain, eyes fixed on the top, and climbing.

The word is almost always used when the goal in question is something competitive, honorable, or difficult to reach — a profession, a title, a political office, a championship. You wouldn't normally call someone an aspirant if they simply want a glass of water. The ambition has weight to it.

There is also an element of seriousness and dedication baked into the word. An aspirant isn't merely a daydreamer. They are someone who is genuinely pursuing the goal — preparing, working, sacrificing.

These examples will help you see how the word feels in real use:

  • "The young aspirant practiced piano for eight hours a day, dreaming of performing at Carnegie Hall."
    She hasn't made it yet, but she is seriously working toward that dream.
  • "Dozens of aspirants lined up outside the audition hall, each hoping to win the lead role."
    Multiple people are all competing and trying to reach the same goal.
  • "As a political aspirant, he spent years building relationships within his community before running for office."
    He is pursuing political power — seriously and actively, but hasn't won it yet.
  • "The monastery accepted only three aspirants that year, each of whom wanted to become a monk."
    People at the very beginning of a formal journey toward a respected role.
  • "She was widely regarded as the most talented aspirant for the position of chief editor."
    Among those competing for a prestigious role, she stood out.

This is important, because a few words can seem similar but mean different things:

  • An aspirant is not a winner or an achiever — the moment the goal is reached, the word no longer applies. A person who becomes a champion was an aspirant before the victory.
  • An aspirant is not just a dreamer. A dreamer may wish without acting. An aspirant is doing something about it.
  • An aspirant is not yet a candidate in the formal sense. A "candidate" is usually someone who has officially entered a process — applied, been nominated, or declared. An aspirant may still be in the earlier stage of simply preparing and wanting.

The plural is simply aspirants — used when referring to more than one person striving toward a goal.

"The program attracted aspirants from across the country."
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Aspirant" is a formal word. You will most often see it in:

  • Journalism and news articles ("political aspirants," "young aspirants in the field of medicine")
  • Literature and formal writing
  • Official or academic contexts

In everyday casual conversation, people might instead say "someone who wants to be..." or use words like "hopeful" or "wannabe" (though "wannabe" has a slightly mocking tone). "Aspirant" carries dignity and respect — it treats the person's ambition as something real and serious.
An aspirant is a person who has a serious, active ambition to reach a high or prestigious goal — someone who is striving hard to get there, but has not yet arrived.
